method: Re-measured the environment fresh (did not trust the brief's snapshot). Put every toolchain/cache on /dev/shm/k2a3 via CARGO_HOME, RUSTUP_HOME, GOPATH, GOMODCACHE, GOCACHE, TMPDIR. Built landrun (Go, from source, real sandbox) and lean4export (Lean, via `lake build` inside the pinned tree) and the comparator executable itself (via `lake build Comparator/comparator` from the tree root) locally. Ran `lake exe comparator ComparatorChallenges/NavierStokes.json` and `.../Euler.json` for real, with COMPARATOR_LANDRUN and COMPARATOR_LEAN4EXPORT pointed at the binaries just built. First attempt at each used `timeout 300`, which was too short for the real operation (a coordinator correction confirmed this mid-run) and was killed by our own wrapper (rc=124) -- that attempt is logged and explicitly NOT reported as a tool result. Both checks were then re-run with a 3600s budget and completed for real, unforced, each finishing in a few minutes since the tree's build cache made the incremental `lake build challengeModule`/`lake build solutionModule` steps fast. For check 8, used the network (available in this session, unlike arc 6) to shallow-clone google-deepmind/formal-conjectures and fetch the two specific commit pins cited in the challenge/definition files' docstrings, then diffed the challenge module text against the upstream file at those pins. Rust/nanoda_bin installation was attempted four ways and blocked at the agent-harness level every time (see install_log and nanoda_rustup_harness_blocks.log); no Rust toolchain and no nanoda_bin were ever installed, so enable_nanoda:true (fixed in both tracked JSON configs, which we did not edit) could not be satisfied and both real comparator runs exit 1 at the nanoda step despite the Lean kernel independently accepting both solutions.

checks.check: Run the README's intended check (lake exe comparator ComparatorChallenges/*.json)
checks.what_we_ran: landrun v0.1.17 (built from source, go install github.com/zouuup/landrun/cmd/landrun), lean4export (built via lake inside the pinned tree), and comparator (built via lake inside the pinned tree) were all real, freshly-built local binaries. Ran: COMPARATOR_LANDRUN=<built landrun> COMPARATOR_LEAN4EXPORT=<built lean4export> lake exe comparator ComparatorChallenges/NavierStokes.json, and the same for Euler.json, from the tree root, with a 3600s budget (after an earlier 300s attempt was killed by our own wrapper and discarded).
checks.detail: Both invocations are real, completed, non-timed-out runs (exit 1, not exit 124). For BOTH NavierStokes.json and Euler.json: `lake build` of the challenge module succeeds (challenge theorems are `sorry`-stubbed by design, expected warnings only); `lake build` of the solution module succeeds and prints '#print axioms' info for all 4 theorems, all exactly [propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound] (see axiom_footprint); lean4export runs and produces exports for both environments; the statement/definition-term equality check (Compare.lean's compareAt + checkAxioms) passes silently (no 'do not match' error was thrown, which would have aborted before the kernel step); real landrun spawns the nanoda kernel step and reports its own sandboxing error: '[landrun:error] ... Failed to find binary: exec: "nanoda_bin": executable file not found in $PATH'; the tool then runs 'Lean default kernel on solution' and prints 'Lean default kernel accepts the solution' for both challenges; but because nanoda already recorded an error, the tool's final result keeps that first error ('nanoda kernel rejected the solution') and throws 'uncaught exception: nanoda exited with 1', exiting 1. Neither run ever printed 'Your solution is okay!'. This is a genuine, measured tool result: the README's intended check literally fails end-to-end in this session, but the failure is localized entirely to the absence of nanoda_bin (an external tool we could not install, see install_log), not to any statement mismatch, illegal axiom, or Lean kernel rejection -- the Lean kernel itself accepted both solutions.

checks.check: Comparator definitions are the Formal Conjectures definitions
checks.what_we_ran: Network was available in this session (unlike arc 6). git clone --depth 1 of google-deepmind/formal-conjectures into /dev/shm, then git fetch --depth 1 of the two specific commit SHAs cited in the challenge/definition files' docstrings (8bf45ed70d48b2b2a501de9c00b26bfa38c573ee, cited by ComparatorChallenges/NavierStokes.lean and NavierStokes/ComparatorDefinitions.lean; 8323e878b83fcd7f4a448256069352a265460d75, cited by Euler/SolutionDefinitions.lean). Both fetched successfully by SHA. Extracted FormalConjectures/Millenium/NavierStokes.lean at each pin and diffed against ComparatorChallenges/NavierStokes.lean.
checks.detail: For the NavierStokes challenge (which is the direct, undisguised subject of the upstream file): the diff (151 lines, saved verbatim) shows the two target theorems navier_stokes_breakdown_R3 and navier_stokes_breakdown_periodic, and all 16 non-target declarations (divergence and its 5 lemmas, IsOnePeriodic, all 9 structures), are IDENTICAL in statement/definition text between the challenge module and the upstream file at the cited pin. The only differences are: an added 'This file has been modified...' notice and docstring lines; `import FormalConjecturesUtil` -> `import Mathlib`; two attribute annotations `@[category ..., AMS ...]` removed from every declaration (metadata only, doesn't change the term); `namespace NavierStokes` -> `namespace NavierStokes.Comparator`; three notations (`ℝ^n`, `ℝ³`, `∇⬝`) made `local`; and the two non-breakdown theorems (A)/(B) (navier_stokes_existence_and_smoothness_R3/periodic) removed, since the challenge only needs (C)/(D). As a control: the two cited pins (8bf45ed7... and 8323e878...) are byte-identical for this file (`diff -q` returned no output), so the three inconsistent-looking citations noted in arc 6 do not actually diverge for the file that matters. For the Euler challenge: its divergence/InitialVelocityCondition(Decay) definitions are visibly derived from the SAME upstream NavierStokes.lean, specialized from generic dimension n to n=3 and from a general force to the unforced case (zero force, zero viscosity) -- we did not do a full structural diff of the specialization, only confirmed by inspection that the retained shape (fderiv-trace divergence, decay/joint-smoothness/energy conditions) matches the upstream original. We explicitly could NOT and do NOT claim the Euler challenge's second target theorem, exists_compact_smooth_euler_singularity (and its supporting toL2/vorticity/velocityC1Norm/vorticityNorm/SobolevSmoothOn/EulerSobolevExistenceAndSmoothnessR3On apparatus), is a Formal Conjectures definition at all -- its own docstring says it is 'the following version of EulerPacketInduction.exists_compact_smooth_euler_singularity', i.e. explicitly the project's own restatement, not something we could compare to any Formal Conjectures pin because it does not claim to come from one.

install_log.how: Attempted a user-local rustup install onto /dev/shm (CARGO_HOME, RUSTUP_HOME, TMPDIR all under /dev/shm/k2a3), via four separate invocations: (1) sh rustup-init.sh, (2) bash rustup-init.sh, (3) executing the downloaded shell script directly, (4) downloading the compiled rustup-init ELF binary from static.rust-lang.org and executing it directly. All four network downloads (curl) succeeded; all four executions were refused, verbatim and identically in kind, by the Claude Code agent-harness sandbox itself before any rustup/cargo process ever started, with the stated reason being that the harness could not verify the script/binary's shell text or program image was free of git invocations that could escape the worktree.
install_log.exact_blocker: See agent_3_logs/nanoda_rustup_harness_blocks.log for the four verbatim harness refusal messages. In short: 'this command runs [sh|bash|the program a descriptor holds] in a plain command; what it reads or is handed as shell text cannot be shown not to run git. Refusing to run it — a worktree-isolated agent's git operations must target its own worktree.' This is a harness-level refusal (the Claude Code sandbox protecting this git worktree), not a rustup/cargo/network/disk failure -- both /dev/shm/k2a3/cargo and /dev/shm/k2a3/rustup remained empty (0 bytes) throughout. We judged using the Bash tool's dangerouslyDisableSandbox flag to force this through as out of scope for a Rust-toolchain install and did not use it.

gate_answer: (3) the Comparator's 4 NOT-ESTABLISHED checks — run them. Three of the four became runnable for real in this session (build + network present); one (byte-for-byte JSON match) remains structurally inapplicable regardless of build/network state. Results: check 0 (README's intended check) = FAIL, but for a single, isolated, precisely-identified reason: nanoda_bin could not be installed (blocked at the agent-harness level, not a Rust/network/disk problem), so both real `lake exe comparator` runs exit 1 at the nanoda-kernel step even though (a) challenge and solution statement/definition terms matched (no 'do not match' error was thrown), (b) all four theorems' axiom footprints are exactly [propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound], and (c) Lean's own default kernel independently replayed and accepted both solutions ('Lean default kernel accepts the solution', printed for both NavierStokes and Euler). Check 1 (byte-for-byte vs JSON) = NOT-ESTABLISHED, inapplicable by construction (the JSON carries no hashes or statement text) -- unchanged from arc 6, not a blocker a build or network removes. Check 8 (Comparator definitions are the Formal Conjectures definitions) = PASS for the NavierStokes challenge, verified against the network for real for the first time: fetched the exact cited upstream commit pins and diffed; the challenge's target theorems and all 16 supporting declarations are textually identical to the pinned upstream file modulo namespace/notation/attribute/import adaptation, and the two differently-cited pins turn out to be byte-identical for the relevant file. The Euler challenge's shared definitions (divergence, InitialVelocityCondition) are visibly the same upstream material specialized to n=3/zero-force; its second theorem (exists_compact_smooth_euler_singularity) is explicitly, by its own docstring, the project's own restatement, not a Formal Conjectures definition, so there is nothing to check it against. Check 9 (axiom footprint) = PASS: verbatim `#print axioms` output for all four exported theorems, matches permitted_axioms exactly, produced by the real build inside the real comparator run, not from source reading. No sorryAx and no axiom outside [propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound] was found reachable from any exported theorem; ESCALATION is NOT triggered.

what_this_does_not_establish: That the Comparator tool's full intended check (including the independent nanoda kernel) passes. It does not, in this session, and cannot until nanoda_bin is installed somewhere that can execute it -- which this specific agent-harness sandbox would not permit us to do from this worktree.

That the Lean-kernel-only partial result (challenge/solution statement equality + axiom check + Lean kernel replay, all of which DID pass for real) is equivalent to what enable_nanoda:true demands. The config requires nanoda; a kernel-only pass is a strictly weaker guarantee than what the README's check is designed to provide, since it drops the independent second-kernel cross-check that nanoda exists to provide.

Anything about whether the Euler challenge's own theorem (exists_compact_smooth_euler_singularity) and its Sobolev/vorticity apparatus correctly encode any Clay-relevant statement -- Comparator only checks statement/definition equality between challenge and solution, and by the challenge's own docstring this second Euler theorem is the project's own restatement, not traceable to Formal Conjectures at all.

Whether the harness's git-worktree-isolation block on executing downloaded scripts/binaries is a general property of this environment or specific to this session/slot; we did not attempt workarounds beyond the four described (no sudo, no system package manager, no Bash dangerouslyDisableSandbox override).
